head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sort by start; overlapping ranges become neighbours
A gap before this range: a new connected group starts
Each merged block goes to group 1 or 2 independently: 2^comps ways, computed with modular exponentiation

p: Overlapping ranges must be in the same group, so each connected block of overlapping ranges is placed entirely in group 1 or group 2: two choices per block, multiplied across blocks.

2580.takeaway: Count merged overlapping blocks; the answer is 2^blocks (mod 10⁹+7).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: BFS (Breadth-First Search) one level per pass
The k-th largest sum: sort descending, take index k − 1

p: Sorting all level sums costs O(L log L) for L levels. A min-heap of size k would be O(L log k), but L is at most n, so sorting is simple and fast enough.

bullets: Space: O(w) for the queue plus O(L) for sums.

2583.takeaway: BFS level sums, sort descending, take the k-th.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: First and last characters are vowels (substring membership in a short string)
Counts the words passing the test (True is 1)

p: Negative indexes count from the end, so `w[-1]` is the last character regardless of length, and it also works for one-letter words like `u`.

bullets: Space: O(range length) for the slice.

2586.takeaway: Count words in [left, right] whose first and last letters are vowels.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Ascending order; the permutation is built by matching each position with a larger value
Index of the smallest element not yet matched with a bigger one; also the greatness so far
Two pointers over the same sorted array
The current value can be placed in front of the unmatched element nums[i], beating it

p: Greatness counts positions where the permuted value exceeds the original. Using each value only to beat the smallest value it can beat saves the larger values for beating larger ones, which maximises the number of pairs (like the 'assign cookies' greedy).

2592.takeaway: Sort and run two pointers: each value beats the smallest unmatched one if it is strictly bigger.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Remainder class of x (Python's % is non-negative for a positive divisor, so negatives work)
Adding or subtracting `value` keeps the remainder
How many numbers belong to each remainder class
To make the number `mex`, we need some element of remainder `mex % value`, each used once
Use up one element and move to the next target

bullets: Remainder 4 is exhausted at target 4: the smallest missing value is 4.

p: Each operation adds or subtracts `value`, so an element can become any number with the same remainder (that is non-negative). A target m can be formed if some unused element has remainder m mod value, so only the counts per remainder matter.

2598.takeaway: Count elements per remainder mod value; build 0, 1, 2, … consuming one element of the matching remainder each time.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Process hens left to right; grains on the left of a hen are handled first
Can all grains be eaten within time t? Greedy: each hen covers the leftmost uneaten grains it can reach
Feasibility check for the binary search
Distance to the leftmost uneaten grain, when it is to the left of the hen

After going left by d, the hen can either return and go right (cost 2d to come back to its start, leaving t − 2d to go right) or go right first and come back (the right trip costs (t − d)/2 out and back); take the better
Marks every grain within the hen's coverage as eaten
A larger time never hurts, so feasibility is monotone

blocks.h: Why must the leftmost grain be covered first?
p: The leftmost uneaten grain can only be reached by the current hen or hens further right. Letting the current hen cover it, extending as far right as its remaining time allows, is optimal by an exchange argument, and processing hens left to right never wastes coverage.

2604.takeaway: Binary search on time; greedy per hen from the left, considering 'left first then right' versus 'right first then left'.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Running maximum, so conversion value of position i is x + (max of prefix)
The score of prefix i is the sum of conversion values up to i, kept as a running total
Prefix sum of a derived array

p: The score of the prefix ending at i equals the previous prefix's score plus the new conversion value. Keeping the running total avoids recomputing sums.

2640.takeaway: Running maximum and running total: score[i] = score[i−1] + nums[i] + max(nums[:i+1]).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Chooses the row index with the most ones; the key is a tuple (ones, −index), so ties are broken in favour of the smaller index
Number of ones in a 0/1 row

bullets: Both rows have one 1; the key (1, 0) is larger than (1, −1), so row 0 wins: `[0, 1]`.

p: `max` picks the largest key. For equal counts it must pick the smallest index, which is the largest −i.

2643.takeaway: max() with key (ones, −index): the most ones, ties go to the smaller row index.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Value → its cell, built once so each painted number is located in O(1)
How many cells of each row / column are already painted
A row (n cells) or a column (m cells) is completely painted
Index of the first painting that completes a line

p: Searching the matrix for each value costs O(m·n) per painting. With the dict, each painting is O(1), so the whole process is O(m·n) to build and O(len(arr)) to simulate.

2661.takeaway: Map value → cell, count painted cells per row and column, stop when a count reaches the line length.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Internal nodes, bottom up (nodes are 1-indexed, stored at cost[i − 1])
Heap-style tree stored in an array
Costs of node i's left and right children (indices 2i and 2i + 1 in 1-indexed form)
To equalise the two child paths, increment the smaller one by the difference
The node's accumulated path cost going down now equals the larger child's path cost

p: `n = 7`, `cost = [1,5,2,2,3,3,1]` (a perfect binary tree):

Making all root-to-leaf sums equal means, at every node, the two subtrees must have equal best path sums. Fixing the lowest nodes first and passing the larger path cost up keeps each decision local, and increasing the smaller side by exactly the difference is the cheapest way.

2673.takeaway: Bottom-up on the array-stored tree: add |left − right| to the answer and pass max(left, right) upward.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Chained assignment: both ends become the smaller character, the smallest change that makes them equal

p: `"egcfe"`:

Every pair must become equal using the fewest operations, so one of the two characters is replaced. Choosing the smaller of the two gives the lexicographically smallest palindrome at each pair independently.

2697.takeaway: Two pointers: set both ends to the smaller character.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Processes the LAST query first: the last write to a cell is the one that remains
Rows / columns already fixed by a later query
An earlier overwrite of the same row is completely hidden by the later one
A row write contributes val to every cell NOT already covered by a later column write: n − (number of fixed columns) cells

p: `n = 3`, processed from the last query to the first:

Each cell ends with the value of the last query touching its row or column. Going backwards, a query's visible cells are exactly those whose row and column weren't fixed by later queries. Each row/column counts once, so the work is O(q) instead of simulating the n×n matrix.

2718.takeaway: Process queries in reverse; each first-seen row/column adds val × (cells not yet covered by the other direction).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum money to get j walls painted, counting walls painted by the free painter too
Hiring the paid painter for wall (cost c, time t) paints that wall, and the free painter paints t others meanwhile: t + 1 walls total
Cost of reaching coverage j by using this wall as paid; clamped at 0 because covering more than needed is fine
Descending order so each wall is used once

p: `cost = time = [1,2,3,2]`; dp[j] after each wall (index = walls covered 0..4):

blocks.h: Why is the free painter a coverage bonus?
p: While the paid painter spends t time units on a wall, the free painter paints t other walls for free (one per unit). So hiring for one wall covers t + 1 walls. The task becomes: choose a subset of paid walls whose total coverage reaches n at minimum cost, a knapsack.

2742.takeaway: Knapsack where each paid wall covers time + 1 walls (itself plus the free painter's work).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Each operation changes x and num by 1 each in opposite or same directions; to maximise x, increase x by 1 and decrease num by 1 per step, closing the gap by 2

bullets: Starting from x = 6 and num = 4, one operation (x decreases by 1, num increases by 1) makes them equal at 5. So 6 is achievable, and nothing larger is.

p: x must end equal to num after at most t operations. One operation can decrease x by 1 and increase num by 1, which closes a gap of 2. Starting from the largest x whose gap to num is 2t, t operations make them equal.

2769.takeaway: Each operation closes a gap of 2, so the largest x is num + 2t.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of ways to write s as a sum of DISTINCT x-th powers, using the powers considered so far
One way to make 0: the empty sum
The next allowed power; stops when it exceeds n
Descending, so each power is used at most once

p: `n = 10`, `x = 2` (squares 1, 4, 9); dp after each square:
Iterating s upward would let `dp[s - p]` already include the current power, using it twice. Going downward reads values from before this power was considered, so each power is used at most once.

2787.takeaway: 0/1 knapsack counting over the x-th powers ≤ n.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of distinct values in the whole array: a complete subarray has this many
The window currently contains all distinct values (is complete)
Sliding window with a distinct count
Moves `left` forward until the window is no longer complete; every start position before `left` gave a complete window ending at r
Number of start indexes 0..left−1 that make a complete subarray ending at r

p: `[1,3,1,2,2]`, 3 distinct values:

After shrinking, the window [left, r] is the first incomplete one, which means [left − 1, r] was complete and so is every window starting earlier (larger windows stay complete). That gives exactly `left` valid starts for this right end.

2799.takeaway: Sliding window: after shrinking until incomplete, `left` equals the number of valid starts for the current right end.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Inserts the element that just became far enough (at distance ≥ x) into a sorted list, keeping it sorted
Finds where nums[i] would fit; the closest values are at that index and the one before it
Nearest neighbour in a sorted list
Differences with the successor and the predecessor
Only indexes with at least x earlier positions can pair

blocks.h: Why only the two nearest values?
p: For a fixed nums[i] the closest eligible values on each side are its immediate neighbours in the sorted list. Further values are strictly farther, so checking successor and predecessor is enough.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the searches plus O(n²) worst case for list insertion shifts.

2817.takeaway: Maintain the eligible earlier values in a sorted list and bisect for the nearest on each side.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: One entry per surplus stone: a cell with k stones appears k − 1 times
The cells with 0 stones that need one
Every way of matching surplus stones to empty cells (from `itertools`)
Manhattan distance: the number of single-cell moves for a stone to travel

head: matching of empties to surplus stones
total moves

blocks.h: Why can stones be moved independently?
p: A move transfers one stone to a neighbour, and moving a stone along any shortest path costs its Manhattan distance, with no interference between stones. The total is the sum of the distances in the best one-to-one matching.

bullets: Time: O(k! · k) for k empty cells (k ≤ 8 here).

2850.takeaway: Match surplus stones to empty cells by trying every permutation, summing Manhattan distances.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: One value is more than half the array: it can't all be paired with distinct values
The leftover copies of that value after pairing each of the other n − mf elements with one copy
Otherwise everything can be paired off, leaving 0 for even n and 1 for odd n

blocks.h: Why does only the frequency matter?
p: Removing a pair requires i < j with nums[i] < nums[j], i.e. two different values in sorted order. If no value is a majority we can always pair different values until at most one element remains (parity), and if a value is a majority, the best we can do is pair all other elements with its copies.

2856.takeaway: Majority argument: answer is 2·maxFreq − n if one value exceeds half the array, else n mod 2.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Treat tower i as the peak of the mountain
Heights must not increase going away from the peak: each tower is capped by its limit and by the previous tower
The right slope is built the same way
Sum of all heights for this peak

p: `maxHeights = [5,3,4,1,1]`: heights chosen for each peak position:

Moving away from the peak, a tower can be at most its own limit and at most the tower closer to the peak. Taking the smaller of those gives the tallest allowed height, and tallest is best for the sum.

bullets: Time: O(n²) for n towers (the harder version II needs a monotonic stack for O(n)).

2865.takeaway: Try each tower as the peak and extend both sides with a running minimum of the limits.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Largest nums[i] seen so far (the best i for a given later position)
Best (nums[i] − nums[j]) over pairs i < j seen so far
Best of the first two factors
Use x as nums[k] with the best earlier difference
best uses the diff built from earlier elements only; then diff uses the old top; then top is updated: each variable depends only on indexes strictly before the current one

p: A triplet value is (nums[i] − nums[j]) · nums[k]. For a fixed k, the best choice is the maximum earlier difference (which in turn uses the maximum earlier nums[i]). Keeping the maximum prefix element, then the maximum difference, then the maximum product gives an O(n) solution.

2874.takeaway: Chain of running maxima: max prefix → max difference → max product, updated in that backwards order.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A zero absorbs everything into one element (product 0 ≤ k)
Merge x into the group while the product stays within k
Otherwise close the group and start a new one

p: Merging as many consecutive elements as possible into the current group never makes later groups worse: a shorter group can only leave a worse start for the next. Since all numbers are ≥ 1, the product only grows, so the first violation is a forced cut.

2892.takeaway: Greedy grouping while the running product ≤ k; any zero collapses the array to 1.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Treats each item as the MIDDLE of the triplet
max((… for i in range(j) if prices[i] < prices[j]), default=-1)
Best profit among earlier items with a smaller price; `default=-1` avoids an error on an empty generator
right = … for k > j with prices[k] > prices[j]
Best profit among later items with a larger price
Both neighbours must exist (profits are positive)

p: With the middle fixed, the left and right items are chosen independently, each as a simple maximum. This turns a triple loop into O(n²).

2907.takeaway: Fix the middle item; best left (smaller price) + its profit + best right (larger price).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: sorted(v for row in values for v in row)
Flattens the matrix and sorts all items ascending
The i-th purchase (day i + 1) multiplies its value by the day number

p: Items in each row are non-increasing from left to right, and only the rightmost (cheapest) remaining item of a shop can be bought. Buying all items in globally ascending order respects that rule. By the rearrangement inequality, pairing the largest values with the largest day numbers maximises the total, and ascending order does exactly that.

bullets: Time: O(N log N) for N items.

2931.takeaway: Buy in ascending order of value so the largest values get the largest day multipliers.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The element that ends up at position j after shifting the row by k (the same pattern for even rows shifting left and odd rows shifting right: the equality check is symmetric)
Position j keeps its value after the shift
Every position in every row must keep its value

p: `[[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]]`, `k = 4`: shifting by 4 equals shifting by 1 (mod 3), and the values differ:
bullets: The first comparison already fails, so the answer is False.

blocks.h: Why compare with index (j + k) % n only?
p: A row is unchanged by a cyclic shift of k iff every element equals the element k positions away (mod n). A left shift by k and a right shift by k give the same condition, because shifting right by k is the same as shifting left by n − k, and the row is unchanged under one exactly when it is under the other.

2946.takeaway: A row survives a cyclic shift iff row[j] == row[(j + k) % n] for all j.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Counter of occurrences inside the window
The newly added value x now appears too often; shrink from the left until it appears at most k times
Remove the leftmost element from the counts

blocks.h: Why only the new value can break the window?
p: Before adding x, every value occurred at most k times. Only x's count changed, so only x can exceed k, and shrinking until cnt[x] ≤ k restores validity. The `while` is needed because the leftmost elements may be other values.

2958.takeaway: Sliding window with a Counter: add on the right, shrink on the left until the new value's count is ≤ k.
